title: Notes of Ministry - 98 - January 1981

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 98 - January 19 (2045)/Notes of Ministry - 98 - Januar - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I have been thinking, beloved brethren, of the work of God in our souls. We often place great store on our knowledge, on what we can take in mentally as to the truth. In doing that I fear we often neglect what is inward, substantial, and vital, as to the work of God. I read the scripture Ecclesiastes because it brings to light something that is very mysterious, and the work of God is like that, it is something that the human mind cannot understand. In a way the human mind can lay hold of the truth and it does exercise itself in relation to the truth; there is really no mystery about that; that is just a question of our intelligence and of our learning, our ability to remember things. I would not discredit in any way the reading of the ministry and the understanding of the truth; we need to attend to that side, particularly younger men and younger women need to have a knowledge of the truth as it has been set out for us in ministry; Paul tells Timothy to give himself to reading.

But what I am concerned about, beloved, is that it does not stop there. I think very often what we take in stops in our minds, but what think the Spirit of God would have with us at the present time is what is inward, what is substantial, what is by the Spirit, and that is mysterious. It says, “As thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit”; there is something mysterious about the Spirit; He has taken no bodily form. He took the form of a dove when He came on Jesus, but there is no bodily form as He is with the saints; there is no tangible expression as to the Person of the Spirit in the way of something that can, be seen; there is a certain mystery about that divine Person that is very wonderful. His power is there; His power can be known; but there is a mystery as to His Person and there is a mystery as to His work, and that relates to every one of us, that where the work of God is there is a certain mystery about it, a certain thing about it that cannot be understood. The human mind cannot relate itself to what the Spirit does inwardly in relation to any one of us in whom He is working.

So it says here, “As thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit, how the bones grow in the womb of her that is with child”. I just had in mind to draw attention in the scripture to the mystery of the work of the Spirit, the secret side of it. It is what goes on inwardly; it is the way the Spirit works behind the scenes to produce something that is substantial. The idea of the bones refers to what is substantial in the work of God, what is permanent, what cannot be destroyed, and it is a very wonderful thing to think that where the Spirit of God has wrought something with us in this way of inward formation, that can never be destroyed. No matter what the enemy may seek to do with us he cannot destroy the work—of God; he may get us into all sorts of shameful conditions and states but he cannot affect the work of God; that is mysterious and powerful and it is indestructible. I think we want to learn to value what is going on in secret in our hearts. It says, “even so thou knowest not the work of God who maketh all”, so there is something mysterious about that, dear brethren, that even I do not know myself how the work of God develops in my own personality; it is the Work of the Spirit and it develops as we make room for the Spirit. There is nothing of the work of God developed in any one of us without that divine Person.

I think that in the past we have tended to overlook the Spirit and the importance of His labour with every one of us. I am sure the problems of the last twenty years would not have arisen with us as they did if we had known what it was to make room for the Spirit, to let Him have His way with us in producing something that is inward, that is substantial, that is of God, in our souls. If we had learnt what it was to take in the truth and the ministry (through our minds certainly, because it must come that way) but as working things out with the Spirit, then what is secret, what is mysterious, what is substantial for God would have been more formed in our souls.

This psalm refers to the way David makes room for that in his relations with God. I wonder, dear brethren, how deep are our relations with God? How deep are our relations with the Spirit as He operates with us? I have a feeling we tend to be very shallow in our relations with God. I feel, as knowing one’s own experience, the tendency we have to take things in mentally and let them remain there; but David here speaks of the way he was conscious all the time of his relations with God. Wherever he went, whatever he did, he was conscious of God. He says, “Thou knowest my down-sitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off; Thou searchest out my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways”. I am sure there was not a thing that David did in his personal life, in his own circumstances, but what he was conscious that there was a relation there with God, and I believe, dear brethren, that we want to cultivate that side of things. We want to cultivate surely the side of learning and intelligence—but I think we want to cultivate more and more what it is to work things out with God, as if God was just there all the time, and He is there in the Spirit, forming us and guiding us. David says, “For thou possessed my reins”; you can see the control that the Spirit of God had over David as he developed; as he went through one experience after another he went through it as having a divine Person with him working with him in the way he went through things.

Now the work of the Spirit in a sense is not automatic; I think David gave himself to this. I think, dear brethren, we need to give ourselves more to depth of experience with divine Persons as to every matter of each day. David says, “mine uprising”; when he got up in the morning he would be conscious of God, and when he lay down also. “Thou searchest out my path ... and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways”—I have a feeling that God is more interested in every detail of our lives than we often realize. The very details of the way we live, the way we are in our houses, the way we do our Work, the way the boys and girls are at school, I am sure God is interested in every detail of that; and that is what David sets out in this psalm; wherever he went, whatever he did, God was there, God was in it, and David would make room for that. That is the way David developed, it is the way he grew; it is the way he became a spiritual man, it is the way he became substantial.

I do not suppose Scripture speaks of .a more substantial man than David; he went through deep experiences; he knew what it was to sin most shamefully, but you can see even in that, as we get in other parts of the Scripture, ‘the depths of David’s exercises; he turned everything to spiritual profit. In every experience David went deep. It speaks of a man in the gospels who dug and went deep, and I think that is the secret of David’s power and David’s substance. If there was any exercise, no matter how small it was, he went through it with God. When he was a boy caring for his father’s sheep, and the bear and the lion came, David delivered the sheep. He says, “he arose against me” (see 1 Samuel 17: 35). David would say, ‘I felt the enemy’s power as he turned on me’; David made that a matter of deep exercise, of deep soul searching, that the enemy turned on him, and so he develops power, he learns where his power is; it is in his relations with God, the God who was there all the time; in every detail God was there with him.

David says, “Whither shall I go from thy Spirit? and whither flee from thy presence?” You know, the Spirit is with us all the time; He has taken up His residence in us. The Spirit never leaves us; He may be grieved, we may hinder Him, we may not give Him the place that we should give Him, but He is always there. David seems to express that, that you cannot get away from Him; it is a blessed fact, a wondrous fact, dear brethren, that you cannot get away from the presence of the Spirit. His service is to build inwardly, to produce something that relates to the bones, the inwards of a man, the personality, the strength of a man. This is how persons become spiritual; it is not just that the Spirit comes on them; it is that the Spirit has been working away there through a history—and that is something we need to think of, that all of us are making history, making our own histories, and the Spirit would be with us in that. How wonderful it is when we give ourselves to that divine Person so that that history becomes a spiritual history and there is spiritual formation, spiritual substance, with us.

So David says that neither darkness nor Sheol, none of these things can separate him from the Spirit. Some of us got very far away; some of us have been away for a long time; we got lost; but the Spirit of God was always there, and that is why we have been recovered. That was a spiritual experience that some of us have had of being recovered. It is a wonderful thing to be recovered, to be lost for a time and get recovered; that is the work of God, that is the Spirit.

We need to give ourselves to that, beloved brethren; let us make these things a spiritual experience, let us work through them with God; let us work through them with the Spirit and we shall become spiritual substantially.

So David says, “I will praise thee, for I am fearfully, wonderfully made”; there is something very wonderful about the work of God, the mystery of it, the wonder of it. I might not think much about it, but God is thinking about it and the Spirit is there all the time building it up. David continues, “and that my soul knoweth right well. My bones were not hidden from thee when I was made in secret, curiously wrought in the lower parts of the earth”. There is nothing about us, beloved, no thought, no exercise, no circumstance, no feeling, no desire that God does not know about. David says, “Thine eyes did see my .unformed substance”. I suppose there is a suggestion in that of something that is not pleasant, the working through of things, the unformed substance; when there was no form in it God saw it. He was looking at it; He saw what was potential there. He saw what there could be in the power of the Spirit and what He could build, what He could make that would be of Himself, His own work. So it says, “and in thy book all my members were written; during many days were they fashioned, when as yet there was none of them”. I feel, beloved, that we need to give ourselves to this; as I said, we have come through a time that involved much searching, and how much searching we will yet have we do not know. I have a feeling that the time is not going to be easy. I do not think the enemy will leave us long; I think there will be times of searching for us, times of deep exercise; let us make them spiritual experiences, let us work through them with God, maintaining our relations with Him so that we may acquire spiritual substance, that the unformed substance may become formed so that there may be tangible evidence of His work.

Then David says in verse 23, “Search me, O God, and know my heart; prove me, and know my thoughts; And see if there be any grievous way in me; and lead me in the way everlasting”; it is just David opening his heart to God; , there was nothing he kept secret from God, indeed you cannot keep anything secret from God—not even your thoughts. David worked through them with God and he says, “Search me”; think of David speaking about his inwards, speaking about his unformed substance, and then saying to God, Just search me and see if there be any grievous way in me; and, lead me, the way everlasting. I had just that impression, beloved brethren. I think there is something in it for us if we give ourselves to spiritual experience. Certainly read the ministry, learn the truth, but let us get it down into our inwards and work it out through every experience of our lives with the Spirit, that we may be led in the way everlasting.
There are certain exercises that the believer, young or old, must face if he or she is to advance

spiritually. We have referred to one already today—the exercise of piety. Piety is an important exercise in the life of a believer; there are many others to be faced if spiritual progress is to be made. We have read of Moses, John the baptist, and Paul, in certain circumstances involving a journey—a physical journey in their case, but moral in ours, the exercise of having to do with God where there is nothing to minister to the flesh. It is a necessary and important lesson that the believer must learn, and the sooner the better.
Scripture abounds with men who faced their exercises alone with God. Enoch “walked with God; and he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5: 24), then Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Jacob had to arrive in his journey not only at the thought of Bethel, the house of God, but at El-Beth-el, ‘God of the house of God’, Genesis 35: 7. Samuel as a young lad had to do with God alone in the night when God said to him, “Samuel, Samuel!”, 1 Samuel 3: 10. These men are interesting studies, spiritually and morally profitable.

Here we get it in Moses; God says to him, “Moses, Moses!”, the repeated use of his name showing that God would speak intently to him—and to you. He is interested in you. It is a wonderful thing that God is interested in us. The fact that we have come here today gives God great pleasure—it shows that we are interested in the truth, in Himself, and in one another. Everything that is morally beautiful is seen in Christ, the One who, when every one else went to his own home went to the mount of Olives (John 8: 1). What for? To be alone with God. That involves the mystery of piety—every one else going to conditions of rest and natural satisfaction, and Jesus, in perfect, dependent manhood, going to the mount of Olives in the intimacy of His relationship with the Father. Then, what we sang of, the most affecting thing of all, ‘On that cross alone, forsaken’ (Hymn 302), a Man alone with God, having to do with the whole issue of good and evil, the whole issue of sin and sins—alone with God in regard to it, a matter which no one else could face. That brings into relief His glory as the One who was the great sin-Bearer. John the baptist draws attention to Him, “Behold the Lamb of God” and, “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world”, John 1: 36, 29.

In Moses we see a man who had many lessons to learn. He had to learn what it was to come to a judgment of the world. He was brought up in it. John the baptist was brought up in a protected area away from the influence of the world. He grew up in the desert, away from it all; he was protected from the affinities of man in the flesh. But Moses was brought up in the midst of it all, the world as it then existed in all its awful detail—its enmity against the people of God, the murderous spirit that prevailed there. Is it changed today? The world today is the same—pervaded by a murderous spirit. Paul gives us a picture of it when he says of man “the way of peace they have not known”, Romans 3: 17. Moses had to learn to come to a judgment of it—to make his choice. We have read of the second and third phases in the life of Moses. His life, as recorded in Scripture, is divided into three periods of forty years—the first forty in Egypt, the next forty in the circumstances, of which we have read in Exodus 2, and the third phase the last forty years of the one hundred and twenty years of his life. God was preparing him to be useful for Himself, and that is what God is doing with us today in speaking to us, drawing our attention to certain things. He has in mind that we should be useful for Him, not for this world!

Moses had to come to that; he would say to himself, ‘I am not for this world; I am not going to commit myself to that kind of thing’; When we are young especially—alas, sometimes when we are old too—we may get our eye on the things of the world and think they are very attractive, and perhaps commit ourselves to them. It is morally and spiritually disastrous! Moses had to come to that, to make his choice, and he chose rather “to suffer affliction along with the people of God than to have the temporary pleasure of sin”, Hebrews 11: 25. What a choice that was! It affected not only Moses’ history personally, but the history of the testimony as it then was and the history of God’s people. What Moses came to was that he was not for Egypt and Egypt was not for him.

His lot was going to be with the people of God. Oh, that is a wonderful thing to arrive at in your life, that you are not going to commit yourself to the world and the things of the world, but to the people of God and everything that that means. You can be sure if you do that God will most definitely bless you.

Well, Moses learned certain things and he did certain things with the best of motives. He thought that in slaying the Egyptian he had solved the problem, but he found immediately that he was rejected, even by those he had saved. That must have been a terrible experience for Moses in the history of his, soul. He tried to save these people, and in the very doing of it they would have nothing to do with him. It is seen in the life of the Saviour—“He came to his own, and his own received him not”, John 1: 11. Then Moses comes to this position in the land of Midian, away from the world as he had known it, “and he sat by the well”. It is an important experience in the life of the believer, and one that is absolutely necessary, to know what it is to sit by the well, that is, there is another resource than the flesh. Moses could have drawn on all the wealth of Egypt; he had it all at his fingertips, but he had to learn to get away from it all—for him it was a physical, geographical journey; for us it is a moral exercise to take our place by the well. It means that you have to come to realise that the resource for the believer is the Spirit of God. Romans 8 teaches us these great lessons, the greatness of the Spirit of God, and to make use of the power and resource that God has so freely given.

Moses finds that the priest of Midian had seven daughters who came to draw water, and the shepherds drove them away—those who should have taken care of them. “But Moses rose and helped them, and watered their flock”—that is the mark of a pious man, that he is helpful.

In Corinthians in the list of gifts that Paul gives “helps” is one (1 Corinthians 12: 28). We can all help in anything that needs to be done; perhaps not all by yourself, but you can help. First Moses sits by the well, then he drives away these harmful elements. How many harmful elements there have been; how many there are in our hearts, things you have learned by the Spirit of God to judge that do not belong to the believer—they have to be driven away. Then you can commit yourself to this line of helping. I would love to be in my local meeting as one who helps, not one who hinders—thus you are a contributor, bringing in something that soothes and refreshes. That can only be as a result of sitting by the well. There is a remarkable parallel in John 4 with this passage; the Lord says, “The water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into eternal life”. Then, in chapter 7, “out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7: 38), bringing in things that would bring refreshment to the people of God and help to build them up.

Moses then in chapter 3 goes behind the wilderness, “and came to the mountain of God—to Horeb”, and he is still with the flock. I think this shows, that Moses was not spasmodic in his exercises. One thing that would mark a pious man, a spiritual man, is consistency—a greatly needed thing. A man who sits by the well is marked by spiritual consistency in all his exercises. So Moses leads the flock behind the wilderness, and he comes to Horeb. It is not Sinai there, it is Horeb, God known in grace.

“And the Angel of Jehovah appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a thorn bush”. A burning bush may not have been an unusual sight, but what impressed Moses was that this bush was burning yet not being, consumed, so he became interested and turned aside to see. It is a great thing to become interested in God’s things. God will bless you if you show interest; Moses showed interest and God speaks to him. God has nothing for persons who are uninterested. Everything is, available, of course; it is all there, whether you are interested or not—the truth, the blessedness of its scope and the greatness of it, are available to all, but it is there for you to enjoy if you are interested, and if you show the least spark of interest then God will encourage you. He will give you more and more, till you find, like the prophet, that not only is there water to the ankles, to the knees, to the loins, but waters to swim in (Ezekiel 47: 3–5). There is plenty of scope for spiritual movement and spiritual enjoyment.

So Moses turns aside to see this great sight, which is typical of God as among His people. Moses refers to it, “the good will of him that dwelt in the bush”, (Deuteronomy 33: 16). God is going on with His people, that is the lesson. These thorny conditions might jag you up a bit if you get too close to them, might irritate you. You have to learn to get past the natural features that mark one and another and see that God is going on with His people. The bush is not consumed—everything is not finished, as some might say, everything burnt up, everything gone. That is not so. God is going to see His people through. The Lord says, “And behold, I am with you all the days, until the completion of the age”, Matthew 28: 20. The Lord has pledged His support. I am not saying that He is going to support everything; it is not that at all; but “with you”, I suggest, is the “them” of Matthew 18: 20, “there am I in the midst of them”. It is that kind of person to whom the Lord has pledged His support “until the completion of the age”, and He is not going to withdraw it or He would not be who He is.

What more holy ground could we be speaking of than the greatness and glory of the Person and humanity of Christ, those holy sufferings of which we have sung? As we speak of them we sense that we are on holy ground.

Then God says, “I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”. The reaction of Moses was that he “hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God”. I think that means that Moses knew that in the line of continuing exercise he had certain things to face in his life in order that he too should know this blessed relationship with God that was known by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The Lord says, “God is, not God of the dead, but of the living”, Matthew 22: 32. It is a wonderful thing to be alive. The world is dead, morally dead; it is not life persons are enjoying, it is moral death, and it is going on to final and complete destruction. Moses came to that; Pharaoh’s servants came to it too. They came to Pharaoh and said, “Dost thou not yet know that Egypt is ruined?” (Exodus 10: 7), they knew it was ruined, but at present this is the day of God’s grace. He is not willing that any should perish but “desires that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth”, 1 Timothy 2: 4.

In Luke’s, gospel we have John the baptist, a remarkable man—“And the child grew and was strengthened in spirit; and he was in the deserts until the day of his shewing to Israel”. I think this scripture teaches us that God would say, ‘See what I can produce’. Men say, ‘Look what we have done’, but God can say, ‘See what kind of man I have’. “Jehovah hath set apart the pious man for himself”, Psalm 4: 3. So, “He was in the deserts until the day of his shewing to Israel”. I think that suggests that John the baptist learned what it was to grow up without being affected by adverse influences. We read what his clothing was and what his food was; he learned what it was to grow up, we might say, under God’s influence, because we read, “There was a man sent from God, his name John” (John 1: 6); he moved into his public service from the presence of God. It is a very necessary exercise to see how easily we may be affected or influenced wrongly by some who say this or some who say that. What a thing it is to be in the presence of God and get the divine viewpoint on everything, and from that standpoint to move forward. “Until I went into the sanctuaries of God; then understood I their end” (Psalm 73: 17)—you are thus free from every wrong human influence and learn from God Himself—then you find that that is a basis for what is collective. You meet with persons who have similar exercises and you can fit together in relation to the truth and the things of God.

John the baptist did not form part of the assembly, though he had the distinctive place of being “the friend of the bridegroom”; the Lord says that “he who is a little one in the kingdom of God is greater than he”, Luke 7: 28. John says, “A man can receive nothing unless it be give him out of heaven”. That is in John 3 where the Lord earlier stresses the necessity of new birth, that is, an entirely new source, a new way of thinking, a new way of moving, of doing things. John goes on to draw attention to the greatness of Christ.

That is another lesson we must learn, that “He must increase, but I must decrease”. The believer has to come to it in his history that “Christ is everything, and in all”, Colossians 3: 11. John the baptist arrived at the supremacy of Christ, as unaffected by adverse human influences.

Whether you have been brought up, young friend, in sheltered conditions, in the great favour of a Christian home as seen typically in John the baptist, or whether you are a person like Moses who was of right parentage but then found himself amid all the glory of Egypt, you have to come to it that the only thing of value is experience with God. Paul had come to it—“When God, who set me apart even from my mother’s womb, and called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son in me”, not to me, but in me. A deep, inward work was involved; what an appreciation Paul had of the Son of God! He came to it—and he never left it. It says, “He preached Jesus that he is the Son of God”, Acts 9: 20. Then he says, “nor went I up to Jerusalem”; the natural way of thinking would be to go to the centre of things, where those great men the apostles were. Paul did not think that way; he says, “Immediately I took not counsel with flesh and blood”. Paul maintained that spirit and it coloured his ministry and his movements among the people of God. He never attached himself in any party spirit to any of the brethren. In fact, he told the Corinthians, “I did not judge it well to know anything among you save Jesus Christ, and him crucified”, 1 Corinthians 2: 2.

So he says, “Immediately I took not counsel with flesh and blood, nor went I up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me; but I went to Arabia”. This is of deep significance. It would involve the exercises of Romans 7, arriving in exercise at “I myself”, Romans 7: 25. Later on Paul speaks about Mount Sinai in Arabia which corresponds to Jerusalem which now is. Paul went to these conditions, I think, because he knew that the essential thing was to have to do with God alone. You will remember in the gospels where the Lord took the man out of the village (Mark 8: 22–26). The Lord took him away from it all, away from these influences, .so that he was alone with the Lord.

That is like Paul here; he went to Arabia, and I have no doubt he went through deep exercises there. Then he still did not go up to Jerusalem, he returned to Damascus. Paul would learn a lot at Damascus—he was taken there to begin with after his conversion when the Lord Jesus appeared to him. What the origin of the assembly in Damascus was we do not exactly know, but Paul was taken there and there he learned deep lessons as to the assembly. Later on he formed assemblies, but he had no part in the forming of the assembly in Damascus—in fact, he was going to persecute it. So, he returned again to Damascus, then he goes up after three years to Jerusalem, and it is significant that it says, “to make acquaintance with Peter”, that is, the forging, of intimate personal relationships. Dear brethren, if there is anything needed today among the saints it is that deep, intimate, personal relationships in the truth should be formed and forged and maintained. It is essential. The enemy is very active, seeking to disrupt the saints in their relations together by whatever means he can—local difficulties or whatever it may be.
Then Paul says, “I remained with him fifteen days”; no doubt links would be forged there, so much so that later, when certain matters arose and Paul had to withstand Peter to the face.

Peter took it in the spirit in which it was given and could refer to “our beloved brother Paul”, 2 Peter 3: 15. Peter did not speak about Paul in a derogatory way. Now let us be practical. If a brother speaks to you faithfully when you are set on a wrong course, or your mind is set on certain wrong things that would hinder you spiritually, how do you react? The immediate reaction of the flesh would be that you do not like that person. We need to forge relationships in the truth; John—says, “whom I love in truth”, 2 John 1. Let us set ourselves to maintain these relationships. Paul goes on to say, “I saw none other of the apostles”—it is remarkable that he did not go among all the other apostles. I think it points to Paul’s own distinctiveness and what he received from Christ in glory, not that he was independent of the other apostles for he says he saw also “James the brother of the Lord”. I think that Paul, who had never known Jesus in manhood here, would very much want to learn from James how the Lord acted, how He spoke, how He lived. Paul would be very interested in that, and it would have to do with what he speaks of as “the mystery of piety”, 1 Timothy 3: 16.

What I have said involves necessary individual exercise, because what we are individually must underlie what we are collectively. May the Lord help us to set ourselves in this line of having experience with God as individuals, thereby to strengthen what is of God in the places where we are, for His name’s sake.
P.

When the beloved disciples heard the Lord speaking to His Father in John 17, what happy remembrances of His service to them must have been recalled to their minds as He said, “When I was with them I kept them in thy name; those thou hast given me I have guarded, and not one of them has perished, but the son of perdition, that the scripture might be fulfilled” (John 17: 12). He had already spoken of another Comforter (John 14: 16) of whom He could say, “Ye know him, for he abides with you”. The kind of service which the Spirit was to undertake on their behalf had already been made known in all its fulness by the Lord Himself. How many times He had protected them, for they had continued with Him in His temptations, but on each occasion He had given them some fresh impression of His glory.

They walk through the cornfields and the Pharisees impugn their liberty to eat the ears of corn on the sabbath, but in defending them the Lord shows that He is Lord of the sabbath also (Luke 6: 5). The disciples are accused of transgressing the tradition by eating with unwashed hands and the Lord not only points but that God’s commandments are being transgressed by the accusers, but discloses the great matter of the essential sinfulness of the heart of the kind of man whom He had come to remove for ever from the sight of God by His death (Matthew 15). It is amazing how the natural mind loves to find fault—“Why do ... thy disciples fast not?”, they ask (Mark 2: 18). All the blessedness of the new character of things in Christianity comes to light—a new garment and new skins for new wine—what takes character from the Bridegroom Himself. Our hearts look forward to seeing Him again. What joy they must have experienced as being in His presence; they could not fast in those days.

“Blessed be he who comes in the name of the Lord”, they cry in Matthew 21, and the religious leaders would have them rebuked, for their hearts were harder than the stones which would otherwise have cried out and they are indignant as the children shout, “Hosanna to the Son of David”. But what a blessed answer, which has encouraged His own down through the ages, “Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise”.

We are told that He “Having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end” (John 13: 1) and He says therefore; “If therefore ye seek me; let these go away” (John 18: 8), and that at a moment of supreme pressure.—Blessed Paraclete who had kept them in the Father’s name!

It was not only the disciples as together that He had guarded; such persons as the woman in the Pharisee’s house who had “loved much” (Luke 7), the Woman in Luke 13 who was a daughter of Abraham, and Zacchaeus, a son of Abraham, all came under His gracious service. Even the disciples themselves took on the character of the accuser, but in grace the blessed Comforter could set, all right and could justify Mary’s choice of the good part, the which should not be taken from her (Luke 10: 42): When the disciples would have rebuked them, the little children were told to come to Him, “for the kingdom of the heavens is of such”, Matthew 19: 14. “Let her alone”, says the Lord of the woman who anointed His head, “She has wrought a good work as to me ... What she could she has done”, Mark 14: 6–8. .How, much He appreciated a heart that thought for Himself.

There were other forces from which He preserved them. Satan demanded to have the disciples to sift them as wheat, but the Lord says to Simon, “I have besought for thee that thy faith fail not”. Luke 22: 31, 32. It is wonderful to see that even before the failure the blessed Comforter is speaking of recovery—“Once thou hast been restored, confirm thy brethren”. What would they have done without the constant service of the Paraclete?

What Christ did then on earth He now does in heaven, and the Holy Spirit—“another Comforter”—carries it on down here. It is the same character of service and we can thus learn from what the Lord did all that is available now by way of divine support to carry the saints through for God’s pleasure in the face of every kind of opposition.

I read these words to call attention to the blessed fact that communications of love are given in the disembodied state. It is not only that the spirit of the saint rests in conditions of love, but communications of love continue. The body is not necessary for these receptions, these communications of love, for Paul speaks of a time when he was not conscious of being in the body. That is to say, the body has nothing to do with the matter. He was caught up to paradise and heard unspeakable things, and such were divine communications.

Beloved brethren, how sweet it is to think of it. We know how the Lord delighted to make communications of His love while down here, and how He continued to do so after His resurrection, but the words we have read carry us into the region of paradise, and we find “a man in Christ” there.

How one loves to think of our sister there in that blessed order of manhood—“a man in Christ” no longer.in mixed conditions and trammelled with an earthly vessel. Now she is free from all that, but still competent—blessed be God!—to receive communications from Him, and such communications as our ears have never heard, those of paradise that cannot be uttered in this lower world.

How wonderful to depart and be with Christ, which is very much better, and also to have communications of love continue as never before. How I love to think of it! So in the disembodied state not only do spiritual affections remain, but there will be for our spirits occupation with divine communications, spoken and heard in that holy scene. How it enlarges the thought of being with Christ. So whatever the interval, be it long or short, our spirits will then not only have the consciousness of love, but love’s communications also.
Jottings of a word at the burial of a sister at Exeter in 1938.
(The above connects interestingly with a word in the December 1978 issue, ‘Communications of Love Continue’, and with extracts from earlier ministry in that issue—Ed.)
Dear child of God, tossed by the stormy billows,
Toiling and rowing on life’s troubled sea;
Look up and trust, thy Saviour knows thy weakness,
Upon the mountain top He prays for thee.
At God’s right hand, in highest glory seated,
For thee, poor needy one, He intercedes;
Fear not, the angry waves shall not o’erwhelm thee,
They cannot harm the one for whom He pleads.
He sees thy plight, and though thy faith should falter, He draweth near, He cometh to thine aid,
Speaks to thy heart in words of sweetest comfort—
“Be of good cheer, ‘tis I—be not afraid”.
And lo! His presence calms the storm and tempest,
Brings an abiding peace—in Him confide,
Rest in His love—His faithful love and wisdom,
To His own rest He shall thee safely guide.
Tingwall, Shetland
(The author was largely confined to her home, due to poor health, and the Lord took her in 1915 at the age of 25).

MORNING AND EVENING Each day in the history of Israel was to begin with the offering of a lamb of the first year, without blemish, as a burnt-offering, and each day closed with exactly the same offering (see Exodus 29: 38–42; Numbers 28: 3–8). This is a precious indication of God’s pleasure that the days of His people should be so encompassed, beginning and ending sweetly with thoughts of Jesus. May we be exercised that our days may be like this. It means that as we briefly read and pray, perhaps as we dress, we are thinking of that ‘patient, spotless One’. How refreshing, renewing, and delightful it is to come back to the perfection of Jesus as here obediently and sacrificially for the will of His Father. It maintains us in the appreciation of Himself. One so completely different from what is in the world, and it strengthens us to be here like Him.

Then as the day closes we are to return to the same delightful occupation with Him. Let our days be thus sanctified. The Father’s delight in His Beloved is constant, and He would have us to share it with Him.

The fact that the offering of the lambs was accompanied by an oblation—fine flour mingled with oil—and a drink offering, enriches the thought of engagement with Jesus and His holy character of manhood. It also shows that the Father is refreshed day by day by His saints’ fresh appreciation of Christ.

Many a person might be well up in Scripture, and able to open up all the different parts of it like a science, or a dissected map, and yet that person not really understand, it; because, as another has said, you must be in it to understand it. This you learn by nearness.
